title: Makarska With a Dog 2027: Beaches, Rules, Costs
metaDescription: Makarska with a dog in 2027: official dog beaches, ferry rules, hotel pet fees, summer heat, vet basics and EU pet passport rules for drivers.
content:
## Dog Beaches in Makarska: Where Dogs Can Swim

Makarska has designated dog beaches, called *plaža za pse* in Croatian. They are the only beaches where a dog can swim without a risk of being told to leave.

### Cvitačka: the closest official dog beach
Cvitačka is the last in the row of pebble beaches west of the centre. It lies about 2 km from the town centre. Rocks separate it from the neighbouring beaches, and pine forest sits behind it. The pines give some shade, but the open pebbles get very hot at midday. There are no dependable facilities, so bring water, a bowl and a sunshade for the dog.

### Ramova
Ramova is a second signed dog beach on the coast just outside the main town, reached from the D8 coastal road. Entry is free. Facilities are basic. Treat it as a pebble-and-sea spot, not a managed beach club.

### Baška Voda (Oseka)
About 8 km north, Baška Voda has a marked dog-friendly stretch near the Oseka beach bar. The section runs from the steps about 200 m from the Milenij aparthotel to the steps northwest of the bar. Dogs swim only within this section.

Brela, a little further north, also has marked dog areas, and the Makarska Riviera is the better base on this coast for a dog owner than most Dalmatian stretches. Rules and signage change between seasons, so check for local signs on arrival.

## Are Dogs Allowed on Other Beaches in Makarska?
No, in practice. The main city beach, Donja Luka, and the other central beaches are posted against dogs in summer. Quieter coves along the Riviera are mostly unmarked, but municipal bans apply, and lifeguarded sections are off limits. Skip the central beaches entirely and go straight to Cvitačka or Ramova.

## Dogs on the Promenade, in the Old Town and in Restaurants
The seafront promenade (the Riva) and the old town streets are open to leashed dogs. Pavement and stone can burn paws from late morning in July and August, so walk early or after 19:00.

Most cafés and konobas accept dogs on outdoor terraces. Indoors, the rule is up to the owner of the venue, and many refuse. Dogs are not allowed in food shops or markets. Ask before sitting down and keep the dog under the table on a short lead.

## Dogs in Biokovo Nature Park and on Trails
Biokovo rises directly behind Makarska. Leashed dogs are generally tolerated on trails, but the park authority sets the rules, so confirm at the entrance. Summer is the problem: the limestone offers almost no shade or water, and the lower slopes can exceed 35 °C. Hike with a dog only in spring or autumn, start at sunrise and carry at least 1 litre of water for the dog. Watch for snakes (the horned viper lives here) and for sharp rock that cuts pads.

## Ferries and Catamarans With a Dog
On Jadrolinija, pets travel free of charge. Dogs must be leashed and muzzled, and larger dogs (over 8 kg) stay on the open deck. Small pets under 8 kg travel in a carrier kept under the seat or on the lap, and each passenger may bring one carrier.

On catamarans, dogs over 8 kg go in designated boxes on the open deck. This carries a fee under the official price list, and a reservation is mandatory. The fee is not published as a flat figure, so email or visit a Jadrolinija sales point before travelling. Private catamaran operators often charge 50–100% of the ticket price for a dog. For Brač, the car ferry from Makarska to Sumartin is the easier option, because the dog can stay with the vehicle and the open deck. Carry the vaccination booklet on board.

## Accommodation: What a Dog Costs
Pet fees in private apartments and small hotels typically run €5–€15 per night. Some hosts add a one-off cleaning charge instead. Many apartments refuse dogs outright, so filter for pets before booking and get the fee confirmed in writing. Choose ground floor or a place with a terrace, and a unit with tiled floors and air conditioning. Camp sites around Makarska and Baška Voda usually charge a per-night dog rate, in the same low single-digit to €10 range.

## Summer Heat and the Best Months
July and August regularly reach 30–35 °C with warm sea. Asphalt and pebbles get hot enough to injure paws. The best months are May, June, September and October, when the sea is swimmable and daytime temperatures are comfortable. In July and August, limit activity to early morning and evening, and never leave a dog in a parked car.

## Vet Basics
Makarska has local veterinary clinics, and pharmacies stock tick and flea products. Ticks and sandflies are present in the hinterland and in long grass, so use tick prevention before arrival. For emergencies outside normal hours, the nearest larger vet service is in Split, about 60 km northwest. Keep a copy of vaccination records on your phone. Dogs must be microchipped and leashed in public.

## EU Pet Passport Rules for Driving to Croatia
Every dog entering Croatia needs three things: an ISO microchip, a valid rabies vaccination given at least 21 days before travel (after the chip), and an EU pet passport or, for non-EU owners, an animal health certificate. Up to five pets can travel non-commercially per person. Croatia does not require tapeworm treatment for dogs.

Driving south from Makarska toward Dubrovnik, the route crosses a short coastal stretch of Bosnia and Herzegovina at Neum. Keep the pet passport in the car, because a border check can ask for it.

## Verdict: How Dog-Friendly Is Makarska?
Makarska is dog-friendly on a practical level, not a perfect one. Two official dog beaches within a few kilometres, a dog stretch at Baška Voda, a leash-friendly promenade and terraces that welcome dogs make it one of the better Dalmatian bases. The limits are heat, bans on the main beaches and the lack of shade at the dog beaches. Rating: 3.5 out of 5 in summer, 4 out of 5 in May, June, September and October.

faq.question: Does Makarska have an official dog beach?
faq.answer: Yes. Cvitačka, about 2 km from the centre, is the official dog beach, and Ramova is a second signed dog beach. Baška Voda, about 8 km north, has a marked dog section near the Oseka beach bar.

faq.question: Are dogs allowed on the main beaches in Makarska?
faq.answer: No, not on the central city beaches in the summer season. Use Cvitačka, Ramova or the Baška Voda dog stretch instead. Check the signs on arrival.

faq.question: Can dogs travel on Jadrolinija ferries and catamarans?
faq.answer: Pets travel free on Jadrolinija ferries, leashed and muzzled, with larger dogs on the open deck. On catamarans, dogs over 8 kg go in deck boxes for a fee and need a prior reservation.

faq.question: How much do accommodations charge for a dog in Makarska?
faq.answer: Typically €5–€15 per night, or a one-off cleaning fee. Many apartments do not accept dogs, so confirm the fee and the rule in writing.

faq.question: What are the pet passport rules for driving to Croatia?
faq.answer: The dog needs a microchip, a rabies vaccination given at least 21 days before travel, and an EU pet passport or animal health certificate. Keep the documents in the car, particularly if crossing the Neum corridor.

faq.question: What is the best time to visit Makarska with a dog?
faq.answer: May, June, September and October. July and August can reach 30–35 °C and the pavement and pebbles are too hot for paws at midday.

quickAnswer: Makarska is moderately dog-friendly. It has an official dog beach at Cvitačka, about 2 km from the centre, plus Ramova and a dog stretch at Baška Voda. Dogs are welcome on the promenade and on restaurant terraces if leashed. Most town beaches ban them. Visit in May, June, September or October.
